title: Latent heat and multistage changes
objectives: Use Q=mL for phase transitions; determine partial melting; combine sensible and latent stages without skipping boundaries.
difficulty: Beginner through application; final question is a challenge
instructions: Show the equation, substitution, arithmetic and units for numerical answers. Explain physical meaning. Use given constants. Retain intermediate digits and round final answers as requested; for unspecified precision, accept sensible rounding. Graphs and data are simulated educational models.

questions.prompt: Which equation models melting at constant temperature: Q=mcΔT or Q=mL? Explain.
State one valid unit of latent heat L and explain why it has no temperature-change denominator.
For water condensing at its boiling temperature under fixed pressure, is Q positive or negative for the condensing water? What about the surroundings receiving that heat?
A 30 g ice sample is already at 0 °C. Is “at 0 °C” enough to conclude it is all liquid? Explain.
Find the heat required to melt 25.0 g ice at 0 °C to water at 0 °C near 1 atm. Use L_f=334 J/g.
A 60.0 g ice sample at 0 °C receives 6680 J near 1 atm. Use L_f=334 J/g and neglect other energy terms. Find liquid mass, remaining ice and final temperature.
How much heat is released when 3.00 g water vapor condenses to liquid at 100 °C near 1 atm? Use L_v=2260 J/g. Give the signed heat for the water too.

Challenge: Heat 15.0 g ice from −8.0 °C to liquid water at 12.0 °C near 1 atm. Use c_ice=2.10 J/(g·°C), L_f=334 J/g and c_water=4.18 J/(g·°C). Neglect losses and container energy. Show all three stages and total heat.
